section.title: Warning examples
section.p: The last few sections gave us strong tools:
Fermat's theorem, Rolle's theorem, the Mean Value Theorem,
the first derivative test, the second derivative test, and l'Hospital's Rule.
Each one has a boundary. A theorem is useful only when its hypotheses are true. This section collects the warning examples in one place, so the rules are easier to use and harder to misuse.

subsection.p: There is no contradiction. Fermat's theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint, the graph only has to be compared with points on one side. It can be best or worst without flattening out.

note.title: Key take-away

subsection.p: That is why the closed interval method always checks endpoints separately.

Three different outcomes are possible.

paragraphs.title: A local minimum
paragraphs.p: The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But x^4\ge 0 for every x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

paragraphs.title: A local maximum
paragraphs.p: The test again gives no conclusion. But -x^4\le 0 for every x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

paragraphs.title: No local extremum
paragraphs.p: But x^3 is increasing through 0. There is no local maximum or local minimum.

figure.caption: When f'(0)=0 and f''(0)=0, the second derivative test is silent.

subsection.p: The moral is short:
Most often, we return to the first derivative test or to the definition of local maximum and local minimum.

subsection.title: l'Hospital's Rule cannot be used on every quotient
subsection.p: l'Hospital's Rule is a rule for the indeterminate forms \frac00 and \frac{\infty}{\infty}.
The first question is always: What form does direct substitution produce?

paragraphs.title: A derivative quotient with no limit
paragraphs.p: Sometimes the original quotient has a limit, but the quotient of derivatives does not.
But the quotient of derivatives is
which has no limit as x\to\infty.

There is no contradiction. l'Hospital's Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

note.title: Key take-away
note.p: If the derivative quotient does not settle, l'Hospital's Rule gives no conclusion.

subsection.title: A theorem-use checklist
subsection.p: The warnings can be compressed into a practical checklist.

table.title: Checklist of conditions before applying calculus theorems

row.cell: Is the extremum at an interior point? Is the function differentiable there?
Is the function continuous on [a,b]? Is it differentiable on (a,b)?
Does f' actually change sign around the critical number?
Is f'(c)=0? Is f''(c) positive or negative, not zero?
Is the quotient really 0/0 or \infty/\infty? Does the derivative quotient have a limit?

subsection.p: A theorem is not only a conclusion. It is a package:
If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

These warnings prepare the chapter review. We now gather the ideas into one working map: how to read shape from derivatives, how to prove global facts from the Mean Value Theorem, and how to tell when a tempting shortcut is legal.
